The day at a glance

Starts in the Paso Robles AVA, one of California's largest, where hot days and cool nights suit cabernet and the rhône varieties; the vineyards run right up to the edge of town and follow Highway 46 West most of the way to the ridge. Over the top the planting stops, and the coastal side is cattle ground down Old Creek to Cayucos, then vegetable fields either side of Los Osos Valley Road.

Worth looking up for

  • Crosses the range on back roads rather than a highway — Highway 46 West over the ridge at mi 15, then Santa Rita and Old Creek Roads down to the coast.
  • Morro Bay at mi 31, with Morro Rock as the landmark and the Embarcadero a few hundred feet off the route.
  • Los Osos Valley Road carries the second half to Avila and Pismo without going through San Luis Obispo.

What to watch for

  • The steep stretch is mi 14.2–15.1, 350 ft at 7.6% to the 1,528 ft summit. "Sustained pitches to about 9%" means the worst continuous half mile averages 9.9% and the worst quarter mile 11.4%; roughly a mile of the day, in pieces, sits at 9% or steeper.
  • A second climb follows at mi 22.7–23.4, 215 ft at 6.0%, on the way down Santa Rita.
  • Between Templeton at mi 7 and the edge of Morro Bay at mi 28 there is nothing but a tasting room at mi 9.6 — 21 miles with no water, food or toilets, and it is the same 21 miles that holds all the climbing. The longest stretch without water is 30.4 mi, from Paso Robles to Morro Bay.
  • Effectively unshaded.

Stops along the way

Mapped in OpenStreetMap and carried in the GPX as waypoints, so they show on a head unit too. Distances are miles from the start. Tap a name for Google Maps, or the arrow for Apple Maps. Not verified on the ground — opening hours and whether a tap actually runs are anyone’s guess. A star marks a stop somebody picked by hand and vouched for, rather than one the OpenStreetMap query happened to return. Everything else here is within a quarter mile of the line; the few that are further say how far.
